name: Réflecteur laser (LRRR)
tagline: I have no engine and no battery, yet I am still working today.
discovery: Observatories on Earth fire lasers at me and time how long the light takes to come back. As a result, we know the Earth–Moon distance to within a few millimetres, and we know the Moon is drifting away by about 3.8 cm per year.
status_note: Still useful: more than 50 years after I was set up, scientists still aim at my mirrors.

presentation.title: Psst… look closely, I might be working right now. I'm Apollo 15's laser reflector.
presentation.body: I'm a science instrument from the Apollo 15 mission. I have no engine and no battery, yet I am still working today.

chapters.title: A very special mirror
chapters.body: I am a panel covered with 300 glass "corner cubes". Their shape sends light back exactly where it came from, whatever the angle. My cousins from Apollo 11 and 14 have 100 each.

chapters.title: Light ping-pong
chapters.body: A laser pulse leaves a telescope on Earth, travels to me, bounces off and comes back: about 2.5 seconds for the round trip. Since we know the speed of light, we can work out the distance.

chapters.title: Why I am still useful
chapters.body: Thanks to me, scientists confirmed that the Moon is slowly drifting away from Earth: about 3.8 cm per year, roughly as fast as your fingernails grow. My measurements are also used to test Einstein's theory of gravity.

quiz.question: How do scientists measure the Earth–Moon distance with this reflector?
choices: By sending a laser and timing its return
With a very long tape measure
quiz.explanation: Light makes the round trip in about 2.5 seconds. Knowing its speed, we calculate the distance.

quiz.question: How far does the Moon drift away from Earth each year?
quiz.explanation: About 3.8 cm per year: roughly as fast as our fingernails grow.

sources.label: NASA SP-289, Apollo 15 Preliminary Science Report (1972)
